title: RCMP officer involved in 2016 collision found not guilty of dangerous driving
article: Constable Michelle Phillips has been found not guilty of dangerous driving causing death and dangerous driving causing bodily harm in a 2016 incident that left one man dead.
Justice J.T. McCarthy made his decision Friday after a four-day trial at the beginning of April.
He said that while there was no evidence of Phillips attempting to swerve or break, the Crown "failed to establish that Cst. Phillips' deviation from the norm amounts to a marked departure."

"I find that the accused's brief departure in this instance, given her overall reasonable manner of driving, is best described as action of momentary inattention, albeit one resulting in the gravest of consequences," said McCarthy.

On the evening of Aug. 21, 2016, multiple witnesses said Tracy Lyle Janvier, 41, was walking down Highway 881, south of Anzac. Phillips was responding to a 911 call that a man matching Janvier's description was walking on the road.
A dispatch call from Joseph Lewis, who had been driving along Highway 881, said someone dressed in black was walking in the southbound lane and that the man tried jumping in front of his truck.
An autopsy found Janvier was intoxicated that evening.
Phillips was responding to the call when she was told a truck had hit Janvier.

Phillips told the court in April that she believed the to incidents were related and that dispatch told her the collision was approximately five to 10 kilometres from Anzac, when it was actually 30 kilometres south of the hamlet.
As she approached the scene, Phillips was driving between 155 and 160 kilometres per hour.

During the trial, Crown, RCMP Cpl. Mark Podesky told the court that had Phillips been driving at 100 km/h, the posted speed limit along that stretch of road, he still believes the collision would have been unavoidable.
McCarthy said he found Phillips to be a "forthright and credible witness," and that he didn't think it was unreasonable of Phillips to believe the collision was closer to Anzac.

As she approached the scene, Phillips noticed several vehicles pulled over to the side of the road. Because she had her lights on, she assumed they had pulled over to get out of her way. It was not until the last second Phillips realized she was about to speed through the scene.

"In my view, Cst. Phillips' failure to recognize that the southbound vehicles represented a potential roadside hazard did not fall below the standard of care expected from a reasonably prudent driver," said McCarthy.
During the trial, the court heard from Alberta's chief medical examiner, Dr. Elizabeth Brooks-Lin, who conducted the autopsy on Janvier.

She said that the injuries could have been sustained from the first collision, she referred back to the evidence indicating Janvier survived the first collision, including blood in his lungs and heart.
She also said while the injuries could have been fatal, she could not say in what order he received each injury.

McCarthy said that although the evidence suggests Janvier was alive shortly before he was struck by Phillips, "it is unclear from this evidence as to whether or not Mr. Janvier was still alive by the end of the 911 call."
James Cardinal, a passenger in the vehicle that first hit Janvier, was injured after the vehicle Phillips was driving hit his hand. He later required 30 stitches for his injuries.
When the verdict was read, Janvier's sister put her head down, crying. Outside the courthouse she told reporters she was "very disappointed."
"Nothing left of him, not a drop of blood left of him, thank you very much," said Marina Nokohoo.
